questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Wage differentials and the pull of the city
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a wage gap draws migrants toward the city
questions.stem: Consultation note: a farmhand from a low-wage district asks why moving to the city would raise her earnings but cost her most of them.

options.text: City wages are lower but housing is cheaper, so net income is the same in both places
options.misconception: ignores the wage gap itself

options.text: Urban wages exceed rural wages, so the gap is what pulls migrants toward the city
Government policy sets both wage levels, so the gap reflects a deliberate transfer decision
options.misconception: assumes wage levels are purely administrative choices

options.text: Migration to the city rarely pays, because city employers refuse to hire people without certificates
options.misconception: assumes certificates bar most city jobs

questions.explanation: The urban wage premium is what makes the move worth it in gross terms, though housing and other prices absorb much of the gain. Government does not simply set both wage levels.
questions.hint: Ask what the gap between place and city wages does.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute the number of working-age residents not in employment
questions.stem: Clinic intake record: a district survey of 2,400 working-age residents records 1,560 in employment, and the clinician is asked how many are not working.
questions.explanation: 2,400 minus 1,560 gives 840 residents of working age who are not in employment. That is the raw excess of labour supply over jobs, the starting point for any equilibrium account.
questions.hint: Subtract the employed count from the total.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how seasonal circulation differs from permanent migration
questions.stem: Ward round note: a clinician records that agricultural labourers leave the district for the coastal towns for three months each year and return for the harvest.

options.text: Seasonal movement of this kind is permanent rural to urban migration in slow motion
options.misconception: conflates seasonal movement with permanent migration

options.text: Such workers are no longer counted as rural residents, so their absence is not migration at all
options.misconception: denies that seasonal absence counts as migration

options.text: Circular movement is migration with a return, so it affects seasonal labour supply rather than settlement
Because the movement repeats, it has no effect on the labour market of either district
options.misconception: assumes repetition removes labour market effects

questions.explanation: Workers who leave for part of the year and return are part of a circular flow: their departure eases seasonal labour supply in the origin and tightens it in the destination, but they do not settle.
questions.hint: Ask whether the workers ever settle where they go.

questions.topic: Age and sex composition of arrivals
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the age and sex composition of an arrival flow
questions.stem: Clinic note: a district health worker has summarised a year's arrivals, recording 480 women and 120 men, with 400 of the women aged 18 to 35.

options.text: The arrivals are overwhelmingly male, so the district should plan for male-dominated services
options.misconception: reads the totals as showing more men arrived

options.text: Most arrivals are women in prime working age, which shapes demand for maternity and childcare
The arrival balance shows birth rates have fallen sharply, since fewer women of childbearing age live here
options.misconception: infers birth rates from arrival composition

options.text: Only 20 per cent of arrivals are women, since 120 out of 600 is one fifth
options.misconception: misreads the totals as a share of all residents

questions.explanation: Most arrivals are women, and most of those are of prime working age, so demand for maternity and childcare services follows from the composition. Arrival counts say nothing about birth rates.
questions.hint: Ask what the arrival breakdown shows.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify how customary occupancy can be recorded in a tenure register

stimulus.body: Tenure recognition surveys record the date on which each household first settled its plot, whether through purchase, inheritance or long occupation, and attach that record to the household's address. Where a household has occupied the same plot for a generation, the survey notes customary occupancy alongside any legal title, so that residents without documents are not excluded from the register.

questions.stem: Consultation note: a resident without formal papers asks the outreach worker how she might still appear on the settlement register.

options.text: She must first purchase the plot at market value before the register will note her presence
options.misconception: assumes purchase is the only route to recognition

options.text: She is eligible only if a neighbouring family can confirm her claim in writing
options.misconception: invents a neighbour attestation requirement

options.text: Registration depends on the plot having been surveyed and mapped beforehand
options.misconception: makes formal survey a precondition of the register

options.text: Long occupation can be recorded as customary tenure alongside legal title, so her presence counts

questions.explanation: The register notes customary occupancy alongside legal title, so a long-term resident can appear without documents. Purchase, attestation and prior mapping are not stated requirements.
questions.hint: Ask what the register records besides titles.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why tenure security raises investment in the dwelling
questions.stem: Counselling note: the clinician is asked to explain why a household that cannot be evicted may invest more in its dwelling.

answer.exemplar: Tenure security turns improvement from a gamble into an asset. When a household knows it will not be removed from its plot, the value of a new roof or an extra room is captured by the household itself rather than lost with the family at the next clearance, so the expected return on such work rises. Where insecurity remains, the rational response is to build lightly and to keep mobility, which is why investment patterns track tenure status closely in settlement surveys.

questions.explanation: Security determines whether the benefits of improving a dwelling stay with the household. With insecurity, effort is spent staying mobile instead, so tenure status shapes investment.
questions.hint: Ask who benefits from the improvements.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the floor area reached by staged additions

questions.explanation: 8 plus 12 plus 15 square metres gives 35 square metres of floor area built up in three stages. Incremental construction adds to what already stands rather than replacing it, so the stages accumulate.
questions.hint: Add the three stages together.

questions.topic: Upgrading a settlement against clearing it
questions.learningObjective: Read evidence that upgrading services in place works
questions.stem: District health log: after a decade of upgrading water and drainage in place, the clinic notes that 90 per cent of households now have piped water, up from 30 per cent.

options.text: The programme is complete, because 90 per cent coverage leaves no further need
options.misconception: treats high coverage as eliminating all need

options.text: Coverage tripled, so the programme must have been achieved by moving households
options.misconception: assumes improvement required relocation

options.text: In-place upgrading raised coverage substantially, so clearance is not the only route to services
The programme failed, since no district has ever exceeded 30 per cent water coverage
options.misconception: invents an unattainable ceiling on coverage

questions.explanation: Coverage rose from 30 to 90 per cent while households stayed put, so retrofitting can deliver services without clearance. High coverage is not complete provision, and no ceiling is implied.
questions.hint: Ask what stayed constant during the programme.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how landmark-based registers can track who is reached

stimulus.body: The outreach team records visits by household identity and location description, such as the blue house behind the grain store, rather than by street address, because much of the settlement is not indexed. Registers maintained this way still allow clinics to track attendance and immunisation, and they can later be reconciled with numbered addresses if the council adopts them.

questions.stem: Outreach note: the mobile clinic records the households it reaches by landmarks and household descriptions instead of street addresses.

options.text: Recording visits without addresses is not permitted, so the team must obtain formal addresses first
options.misconception: claims registration without addresses is unlawful

options.text: Landmark-based records can still track who attends, and may be reconciled later if addresses are adopted
The registers will be unusable once the council numbers the streets, because the two systems differ
options.misconception: assumes later numbering voids the earlier records

options.text: Only households that already hold numbered addresses can be counted in any outreach register
options.misconception: restricts counting to formally addressed households

questions.explanation: A landmark-based register still supports attendance tracking and can be reconciled if numbered addresses are later adopted. Addresses are not a precondition for counting.
questions.hint: Ask what such a register can still do.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: User fees and who stops coming
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a small fee filters out the poorest patients
questions.stem: Prescription note: a clinician records that a clinic introduced a small consultation fee and attendance among the poorest patients fell by a third.

options.text: The fee should be raised, because higher charges would signal that care is worth paying for
options.misconception: suggests raising fees to boost attendance

options.text: The fall shows that poor patients do not value their health enough to attend
options.misconception: blames patient values for attendance falls

options.text: The fee caused the fall, so the clinic should abolish all charges for care
options.misconception: presumes a single cause and a single remedy

options.text: A fee acts as a price barrier, so the burden falls hardest on those with least cash

questions.explanation: A consultation fee prices attendance, and the loss of poorest patients shows the burden landing where money is scarcest. The pattern does not prove the fee was the sole cause.
questions.hint: Ask what a fee does to a visit decision.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Wage differentials and the pull of the city
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the same job pays differently across regions
questions.stem: Health education note: the clinician must explain to a patient why the same job pays more in the capital than in the region they came from.

answer.exemplar: The same work carries different pay in different places because demand for labour is uneven across regions, and the capital concentrates employers, training and networks that the home region lacks. A worker whose skills are scarce nationally can therefore earn more by moving, and the difference between the two pay levels is the surplus that rewards the move and the cost of the journeys, rent and separation it entails. Institutions such as wage floors, licensing and housing policy shift how much of that surplus the worker keeps.

questions.explanation: Pay differences reflect where demand for particular skills is concentrated, and moving captures the surplus the difference represents. Policies affect how much of that surplus the worker keeps.
questions.hint: Ask where demand for that skill is concentrated.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a busy market does not demonstrate full employment
questions.stem: Sanitation note: a health worker remarks that street trading stalls in the district are full every day, which she takes as proof that there is no unemployment nearby.

options.text: The observation is sound, because full stalls demonstrate that labour is fully employed
options.misconception: treats one crowded market as full employment

options.text: The observation is sound, because unemployment measures only the number of registered claimants
options.misconception: restricts unemployment to registered claimants

options.text: The observation is unsound, because crowded stalls can reflect low productivity rather than plentiful jobs
The observation is unsound, because street trading is illegal and so cannot be counted as work
options.misconception: assumes street trading cannot count as work

questions.explanation: Crowded markets can reflect many low-paid workers rather than a shortage of labour, so a busy stall does not show full employment. Unemployment is broader than registered claimants.
questions.hint: Ask what a crowded stall can also indicate.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Plan service capacity for a seasonally changing population
questions.stem: Housing note: a clinician asks how a district should plan clinic capacity when a third of its residents are absent for part of each year.

options.text: Capacity should be built for the peak population, since the absent residents still need care when they return
options.misconception: ignores seasonal absence in capacity planning

options.text: Capacity should follow the seasonal population, because illness demand tracks who is physically present
Capacity should be the same all year, since seasonal variation in need is usually small
options.misconception: assumes seasonal variation in demand is trivial

options.text: Capacity should be set by the number of registered residents, since registration reflects need
options.misconception: treats registration counts as a proxy for need

questions.explanation: Illness demand follows who is physically present, so seasonal absence changes the load on the clinic. Registered counts overstate present population, and the seasonal swing is usually large.
questions.hint: Ask who is present when care is needed.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Age and sex composition of arrivals
questions.learningObjective: Project service demand from the current age and sex profile of arrivals

stimulus.body: Arrival registers record the age and sex of each new resident, and the district profile shows that most newcomers are men aged 20 to 34, with far fewer women in the same band and very few children. Health planners are warned that a young workforce arriving alone will eventually create demand for family services as workers settle and raise families, so present service use understates future need.

questions.stem: Planning note: the district health team is considering what the arrival profile implies for future service demand.

options.text: Present demand understates future need, since a young workforce arriving alone will later create family demand
Only children matter for planning, since they use health services most heavily
options.misconception: assumes children are the heaviest service users

options.text: The sex imbalance shows that migration is driven by men's preferences for particular jobs
options.misconception: attributes migration flows to preferences alone

options.text: Service planning should be based on the current profile, since future populations cannot be predicted
options.misconception: denies any basis for projecting future need

questions.explanation: Today's arrivals are disproportionately young men, whose later family formation will generate maternity and child service demand. Current use understates future need.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to these arrivals over time.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why old neighbourhoods are documented differently
questions.stem: Records note: a clinician asks why residents of long-established neighbourhoods are documented differently from new arrivals.

answer.exemplar: Residents of old neighbourhoods often hold occupancy rights rather than deeds: they came as workers, cleared the land themselves and have held the plot for generations, so their claim is proved by length of possession and custom rather than by a title document. Recognising that record matters for access to piped water, clinics and schools, and for compensation when land is acquired, because a settlement that cannot document its residents has no way to know whom it must serve or whom it must compensate.

questions.explanation: Long occupation produces a real claim that no paperwork records, and documenting it lets a settlement know whom it serves and owes compensation to. New arrivals have no such customary position.
questions.hint: Ask what proof an old resident's claim rests on.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the investment gap between secure and insecure tenure
questions.stem: Survey note: in a surveyed alley, 60 of 120 households with secure tenure built or extended their dwelling, against 24 of 120 households on insecure tenure. What is the difference in percentage points between the two groups?
questions.explanation: Half the secure group invested against a fifth of the insecure group, so 50 minus 20 per cent gives a 30-point gap. Security of possession links to willingness to invest.
questions.hint: Convert each count to a percentage first.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the pattern of additions in a self-built settlement
questions.stem: Clinic housing note: in a self-built quarter, most dwellings are recorded as one or two rooms, and 60 per cent have been added to since the family arrived.

options.text: Incremental building is failing, since most dwellings remain under two rooms after a decade
options.misconception: treats a low room count as build failure

options.text: The additions are wasteful, because families would be better served by complete units
options.misconception: assumes completed units always suit families better

options.text: Most families are near the ceiling of what they can build, so further additions are unlikely
options.misconception: infers a build ceiling from current room counts

options.text: Additions are the normal pattern, since households enlarge as income and needs change

questions.explanation: Dwellings extended after arrival are the expected signature of incremental building, not failure. Room counts reveal no build ceiling, and nothing shows completed units would suit families better.
questions.hint: Ask what a high share of extensions implies.

questions.topic: Upgrading a settlement against clearing it
questions.learningObjective: Explain the preference for upgrading a settlement in place
questions.stem: Consultation note: a resident asks why the council prefers to upgrade water and roads where people already live instead of moving them to new plots.

options.text: Clearance is chosen because upgraded settlements usually need more maintenance over time
options.misconception: asserts upgrading raises long-run maintenance

options.text: Upgrading avoids the political cost of compulsory purchase, which matters more than any other factor
options.misconception: makes political cost the only consideration

options.text: Upgrading preserves households' livelihoods and social ties, which clearance would destroy
Upgrading is cheaper because existing pipes and roads can be repaired more easily than new ones built
options.misconception: reduces the choice to construction cost

questions.explanation: In-place upgrading keeps households, work and support networks intact, while clearance severs those ties. Cost and politics sometimes favour clearance, so they cannot alone explain the preference.

options.text: Outreach visits exceed the recorded addresses, so the register must be overstating formal addresses
options.misconception: infers register inflation from visit totals

options.text: Outreach visits cover 340 of the 780 unrecorded households, so the registry gap is closed
options.misconception: assumes the outreach list equals the household register

options.text: Since 120 addresses are recorded, the remaining 780 families must have declined to register
options.misconception: infers refusal to register from absence

options.text: Most households reached have no formal address, so outreach is doing work registries cannot

questions.explanation: Only 120 of 900 households appear in the register while the team reaches 340, so much of the district is served without formal records. The overlap is unknown, so coverage cannot be computed.
questions.hint: Ask what the overlap between the two lists is.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: User fees and who stops coming
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a small fee cuts attendance among the poorest
questions.stem: Health accounts note: the clinician must explain why charging even a small fee can cut attendance most sharply among the poorest.

answer.exemplar: A fee is a price, and a price of any size falls hardest on people with the least cash and the least ability to postpone a visit, so attendance falls fastest exactly among those whose need is greatest. Because the fee collects a small amount from many well-off patients and excludes a smaller number of poor ones from care altogether, its revenue yield can look adequate while its health effects concentrate in the group it was meant to protect. This is why exemptions and prepayment schemes are usually preferred to across-the-board charges.

questions.explanation: Any charge is a price, and the poorest are least able to pay it, so attendance falls where need is highest. Small fees can still net revenue while excluding the neediest.
questions.hint: Ask who can least afford to pay a price.

questions.learningObjective: Explain what raises a wage for a worker in a scarce skill

options.misconception: assumes legal floors explain most wage gaps

options.text: Her wage would rise because employers in the capital face less competition for workers
options.misconception: reverses the effect of competition for labour

options.text: Her wage would rise because the same work carries a lower social value in her own region
options.misconception: invents a social value explanation for wages

questions.hint: Ask what sets the price of a scarce skill.

questions.learningObjective: Read what persistently low earnings reveal about the labour market

questions.topic: Age and sex composition of arrivals
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a stable total can conceal a shifting composition

stimulus.body: The district's arrival returns record age and sex in five-year bands. Staff note that arrivals in the 15 to 19 band have fallen each year since a school-leaving age change, while arrivals in the 20 to 24 band have risen, and that because the two bands are adjacent the total number of young arrivals has stayed broadly stable even as its composition shifted.

questions.stem: Returns note: the clinic reviews the arrival register and finds the total number of young arrivals steady while its composition shifts.

options.text: The stable total proves that arrivals are governed by a fixed annual quota
options.misconception: infers a quota from a stable total

options.text: The stable total proves that no policy change has altered who is arriving
options.misconception: treats a stable total as evidence of no effect

options.text: A shift between adjacent age bands can leave the total unchanged while changing who arrives
The stable total shows that the age change had no effect on the composition of arrivals
options.misconception: denies a compositional effect from the data

questions.explanation: When one band contracts and the adjacent expands, the total can stay flat while composition changes, as the returns show. That is no evidence of a quota, and it confirms who arrives changed.
questions.hint: Ask how two adjacent bands can offset each other.

stimulus.body: The tenure review compares each household's date of first occupation with the date the plot was first surveyed for legal registration. options.misconception: makes registration a precondition for recording occupancy

options.misconception: assumes customary rights are worth less than title

options.text: The family may be recorded as holding customary tenure despite having no registered title

questions.explanation: The review records customary tenure where occupation predates survey, so a long-standing family is documented without a title. Moving the family or ranking customary rights lower misreads the review.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Upgrading a settlement against clearing it
questions.learningObjective: Explain why authorities prefer upgrading in place to relocation
questions.stem: Planning note: the clinician must explain to a visiting student why authorities may prefer in-place upgrading to relocation.

answer.exemplar: Relocation costs more than the value of the services delivered, because it destroys the asset the resident already holds. A household with a functioning shop, a job nearby and a network of relatives nearby has accumulated something that no new plot at the edge of the settlement reproduces, and clearance transfers that value to whoever ends up with the land. In-place upgrading accepts a lower but immediate gain in coverage, and because it leaves the household's other assets intact it also avoids the resettlement failures that show up later as unemployment and illness among those who moved.

questions.explanation: Clearance severs the household's accumulated livelihood and networks, while upgrading keeps them and delivers services sooner. What residents already hold outweighs the extra cost of retrofitting.
questions.hint: Ask what residents already hold that a new plot lacks.

questions.learningObjective: Decide whether outreach must wait for numbered addresses
questions.stem: Outreach note: the clinic team debates whether it should press for numbered addresses before extending its outreach programme.

options.text: Numbered addresses should come first, since without them no clinic can record who it has treated
options.misconception: makes numbering a precondition for record keeping

options.text: Numbered addresses should come first, because unnumbered areas are usually the poorest

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Wage differentials and the pull of the city
questions.learningObjective: Explain why leaving a village for the city raises income
questions.stem: Counselling note: the clinician must explain to a young patient why leaving her village for the city is likely to raise her income.

answer.exemplar: The city offers a higher wage because employers there are numerous and competition for workers is intense, while the village offers few employers and little bargaining power. For the individual, the difference is the reward for moving and the risk of not finding work, and the deciding calculation is the wage gap net of the costs of relocation: rent, transport, food, and the loss of family help with childcare. Aggregate settlement data shows people move when the gap is wide enough to cover those costs, which is why wage differences matter most for occupations where city demand is concentrated.

questions.explanation: A wide city wage gap covers relocation costs and net pay more when city demand for that skill is strong, which is why movement follows wage differences.
questions.hint: Ask what the move has to cover to be worth it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Wage differentials and the pull of the city
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a wide wage gap still leaves people behind
questions.stem: Wage gap note: the clinician must explain to a patient why a wide regional wage gap still leaves some people in the poorer district.

answer.exemplar: A wide wage gap only produces movement where the difference covers the costs of moving and the risks of the search, and those costs fall hardest on households with least savings. A family that must pay for transport, deposits and school fees in the new place, or that cannot leave work for a time while looking, will stay put even when the advertised pay is much higher. The gap therefore sets the ceiling on what migration can achieve rather than the number who will actually move.

questions.explanation: A wide gap persuades only those who can absorb the cost of moving, so travel costs and lost earnings filter how much it delivers. The gap sets a ceiling on migration rather than predicting it.
questions.hint: Ask what moving costs the household.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why documenting existing residents matters for health work
questions.stem: Clinic record note: the clinician must explain why documenting existing residents matters for public health work.

answer.exemplar: A health programme needs to know who lives where and who is entitled to stay. Where settlements grew without registration, the register of residents is assembled from occupation records, community lists and the accounts of health workers, and those records are what allow a clinic to run, a water connection to be made, or a compensation payment to be calculated when land is taken. Recognising tenure also removes a perverse incentive, since a household that cannot prove occupation has no reason to improve a plot it may be forced to leave, and that is precisely the condition that produces the worst health outcomes.

questions.explanation: Documenting residents allows services and compensation to reach the people entitled to them, and it gives households a reason to improve their plots. Health work is harder where neither holds.
questions.hint: Ask what documentation lets the clinic do.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Age and sex composition of arrivals
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the age and sex profile of a population drives service demand
questions.stem: Service planning note: the clinician must explain to the team why the age and sex of arrivals matters for a health service.

answer.exemplar: Age and sex determine which services a population uses. Children drive demand for immunisation, antenatal and paediatric care; adults of working age drive the largest volume of general and emergency care; older women, who commonly live longer alone, drive more of the chronic disease management that consumes outpatient time. A district whose arrivals are overwhelmingly young men therefore looks light on maternity and child services at first and heavier on them later, and staffing planned on the current mix will be wrong in both directions, over-providing for one group and short for another.

questions.explanation: Age and sex map onto which services a population needs, so a district's arrival profile shapes both demand and its timing. Planning on the current mix alone will misjudge both.
questions.hint: Ask which services each group uses most.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why staged building suits a household better than a completed house
questions.stem: Clinic note: the clinician must explain to a family why building in stages suits their situation better than a completed house.

answer.exemplar: Building in stages ties the dwelling to what the household can actually afford at each moment, so no part of the plan is stranded. A completed house demands the full sum before anyone can occupy it, which for a family with irregular earnings means months of temporary accommodation or a loan at rates they cannot meet. Incremental building also lets each addition match a change that has already happened: a second room when a child arrives, a workshop when the household takes on a trade, water and drainage when the settlement is connected. The result is more money spent on the house overall, not less.

questions.explanation: Staged building matches what a household can afford when it needs it, avoids waiting for a full sum, and lets additions follow real changes. It usually raises total spending on the dwelling.
questions.hint: Ask what the household can afford when.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Upgrading a settlement against clearing it
questions.learningObjective: Identify who is served last under a sequential upgrade schedule

stimulus.body: The upgrade programme will run pipes and drains along existing lanes over three years, and the schedule pauses each street at a time. Residents in the lanes already served will have water and drainage when the programme ends, while those in later streets will not, and the district's own analysis warns that this sequencing will leave the least documented residents at the end of the queue because they are hardest to locate and prioritise.

questions.stem: Programme note: the clinic team is reading the upgrade schedule for the settlement's lanes.

options.text: Sequencing leaves the least documented residents served last, since they are hardest to locate and prioritise
Sequencing is fair, because every lane is scheduled for the same length of time
options.misconception: confuses equal durations with equal outcomes

options.text: Sequencing has no effect on residents, since all lanes are upgraded by the end of the third year
options.misconception: ignores the distribution of benefits over time

options.text: Sequencing matters little, because water connections are made by households themselves
options.misconception: assumes households install their own connections

questions.explanation: With streets served in sequence, residents in later lanes wait, and the least documented are hardest to locate and so served last. Equal durations per lane do not give equal outcomes.
questions.hint: Ask who is hardest to prioritise for the schedule.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess the claim that unregistered residents cannot be counted
questions.stem: Register note: a clinician argues that counting residents is pointless where most households lack a formal address, and asks how the claim should be answered.

options.text: Counting is still possible, since outreach teams can track households by landmarks and reconcile them later
The claim holds, because a count without formal addresses cannot be checked by anyone
options.misconception: assumes unverifiable counts are worthless

options.text: The claim holds, because the settlement has no legal basis for any register of residents
options.misconception: invents a legal bar on local registers

options.text: Counting is pointless, because residents move too often for any household list to stay accurate
options.misconception: treats residential mobility as defeating registers

questions.explanation: Landmark-based lists let outreach teams track who is reached, and they can be reconciled once numbering exists. A count nobody can check is not the same as a count made with another method.
questions.hint: Ask how the team already tracks households.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: User fees and who stops coming
questions.learningObjective: Compute the effect of a price rise on fee income
questions.stem: Budget note: a clinic collects 900 visits a month with a 10-unit fee, and after a 50 per cent price rise visits fall to 600. What is the change in fee income per month?
questions.explanation: Income was 900 visits at 10 units, or 9,000, and after the rise it is 600 visits at 15 units, again 9,000. The change is zero, so this rise neither gains nor loses revenue.
questions.hint: Compute income before and after the rise.
